title: Rescuers Free a Young Whale Tangled in Fishing Line!
summary: Imagine trying to swim with a rope tied tightly around your tail. That's what happened to a young humpback whale off the coast of Massachusetts. It was caught in fishing gear—ropes and buoys that kept it from diving or swimming away. Luckily, some boaters spotted the whale and called for help. A team from the Center for Coastal Studies (CCS) rushed to the scene. These are experts at freeing tangled whales. Since 1984, they've saved over 200 large whales! But this rescue was tricky. The ropes were wrapped around the base of the whale's tail, anchoring it in place. And bad weather was coming, so the team had to work fast. Using a hook-shaped knife on the end of a 30-foot pole—that's as long as a school bus!—they carefully cut the ropes. The whale stayed still at first, then slowly began to move again. It had some wounds from the ropes, but the rescuers think it will recover. This rescue was a team effort. Boaters, the Coast Guard, police, and even a whale expert visiting from Hawaii all helped. It shows what can happen when people work together. But here's the sad truth: every year, more than 300,000 whales and dolphins die because they get tangled in fishing gear. That's like the whole population of a big city! So while this one whale got a happy ending, many others aren't so lucky. Scientists are working on ways to make fishing safer for ocean animals.
why_it_matters: Even if you live far from the sea, the health of ocean animals affects the air you breathe and the planet's climate, so caring about whales means caring about your own future.

background_read: Humpback whales are known for their magical songs and long migrations. Every year they travel thousands of miles from polar feeding grounds to tropical waters to give birth, often passing along the busy coast of Massachusetts (a state in the northeastern USA).

The Center for Coastal Studies (CCS), a marine rescue and research group based in Provincetown, Massachusetts, has a special team that has been freeing entangled whales since 1984, saving more than 200 large whales.

Whale entanglements happen when animals swim into ropes attached to lobster traps or fishing nets. The ropes can cut into their skin, cause infections, and make it impossible to dive for food, eventually leading to starvation or drowning.
Article_Structure: WHO: A young humpback whale tangled in fishing gear, and a rescue team from the Center for Coastal Studies, helped by boaters, the Coast Guard, police, and a whale expert from Hawaii.
WHAT: Using a 30-foot pole with a hook-shaped knife, the team cut the ropes wrapped around the whale's tail, freeing it.
WHERE: Off the coast of Massachusetts, USA.
WHY: This rescue highlights a huge problem: over 300,000 whales and dolphins die each year from fishing gear, showing the urgent need for solutions.

perspectives.description: It was a team effort that saved one whale, proving that when people work together quickly, they can fix a dangerous situation.
Even though this whale was lucky, hundreds of thousands of others die unseen each year, meaning this small rescue doesn't solve the bigger problem.
Scientists are designing special rope systems that break more easily or using ropeless fishing gear to stop whales from getting tangled in the first place.
